faq.q: Can it explain an existing cron expression in plain English?
faq.a: Yes. Paste an expression (or a special string like @daily) into the decode box and it validates it, fills the visual builder, writes a human-readable description, and lists the next 10 run times. It understands the five standard fields plus @reboot, @yearly, @monthly, @weekly, @daily, @hourly and their equivalents.

faq.q: Are the 'next run' times in my timezone or the server's?
faq.a: They're computed in your browser's local timezone, which is shown next to the schedule. The tool warns that server cron jobs usually run in the server's configured timezone (often UTC), so the times you see here can differ from when the job actually fires on a server.

faq.q: Does it handle the day-of-month and day-of-week OR rule?
faq.a: Yes. In standard cron, when both the day-of-month and day-of-week fields are restricted (neither is *), the job runs when either matches — and the next-run preview honours that OR behaviour. It also treats 7 as Sunday in the day-of-week field.

faq.q: Does it support L, # and ? like some schedulers?
faq.a: No. Those are Quartz Scheduler extensions, and the validator explicitly rejects them, telling you they're Quartz-only. The builder and next-run preview use standard Vixie/POSIX cron semantics. You get a visual builder (every/specific/range/step per field), 18 presets, a copyable crontab line with your command, and a recent-expressions list saved in your browser.
